title: What Is Aging in Place? A Plain-English Guide for Older Adults and Families
meta_description: What aging in place means, who it suits, and how staying home compares with assisted living and nursing home costs, using 2025 CareScout and AARP data.
short: Aging in place means staying in your own home as you get older, with the changes and help needed to do it safely.

faq.q: What does aging in place mean?
faq.a: It means living in your own home for as long as you feel safe, confident and comfortable there, instead of moving to a care setting. Most people need some home changes and some outside help to make it work.

faq.q: Is aging in place cheaper than assisted living?
faq.a: Often, but not always. The 2025 national median for assisted living was $6,200 a month. Home changes are usually a one-time cost. But if you need many hours of paid help each week, in-home care can cost as much as or more than a facility.

faq.q: How many older adults want to stay in their homes?
faq.a: In AARP's 2024 Home and Community Preferences Survey, 75% of adults 50 and older said they want to stay in their current homes as they age.

faq.q: Who should I call first for help?
faq.a: Call the Eldercare Locator at 1-800-677-1116 (weekdays, 8 a.m. to 9 p.m. Eastern). It connects you to your local Area Agency on Aging, which knows the home repair, home care and benefit programs in your area.

faq.q: When is aging in place not a good idea?
faq.a: It can be hard when a person needs help around the clock, the home cannot be made safe at a reasonable cost, or the person is isolated with no one checking in. A doctor, social worker or care manager can help you weigh the options.

body_md:
Most of us picture growing older in the home we already know. The neighbors, the kitchen, the chair by the window. That wish has a name: **aging in place**. This guide explains what it means, who it works best for, and how the costs compare with assisted living and nursing homes.

## What "aging in place" means

Aging in place means staying in your own home as you get older, for as long as you can feel confident and comfortable there [1]. It does not mean doing everything alone. For most people it means two things:

- **A home that fits your body as it changes.** That can be as simple as brighter lights and a grab bar, or as big as a walk-in shower or a ramp.
- **Help that comes to you.** That may be a ride to the doctor, meals, a home health aide, or a family member who checks in.

The goal is a home that is safe, easy to move around in, and close to the people and services you need.

## How many people want this

A lot. In AARP's 2024 Home and Community Preferences Survey, **75% of adults age 50 and older** said they want to stay in their current homes as they age. **73%** said they want to stay in their communities [2].

The same survey shows the gap between wishes and reality. About half of adults 50+ said they need a home that supports aging on their own [2]. Many expect to need changes such as grab bars or a safer entry. **64%** said they expect to need a medical alert system [2]. And **44%** of adults 50+ expect they may have to move, often because of housing costs, upkeep or taxes [2].

So the desire is strong. The planning often lags behind.

## Who aging in place is for

Aging in place can work for many people, including:

- **Healthy older adults** who want to plan ahead before a problem happens.
- **People with a chronic health condition**, such as arthritis, COPD, diabetes or vision loss, who need a home that is easier to use.
- **People coming home after a hospital stay** or a fall, who need changes fast.
- **Couples** where one partner is caring for the other.
- **Adult children** who live nearby, or far away, and want a parent to stay safe at home.

It tends to work best when three things are true. The home can be made safe at a cost the family can manage. The person can get the level of help they need. And the person is not cut off from other people.

## Why safety comes first

Falls are the biggest everyday risk at home for older adults. In 2024, falls caused **more than 43,000 deaths** among adults 65 and older in the U.S. They also led to about **4.5 million emergency room visits** [3]. Many falls are linked to things in the home that can be fixed, like loose rugs, dark stairs and slippery tubs. See our guides on fall facts and our room-by-room safety checklist for the details.

## How the costs compare

Here are the national median costs from the **CareScout 2025 Cost of Care Survey**, released in March 2026 [4]. A median is the middle price. Half of providers charge more and half charge less. Prices in your area may be much higher or lower.

| Type of care | 2025 national median | Yearly cost |
|---|---|---|
| In-home non-medical caregiver | $35 an hour | $80,080 (at 44 hours a week) |
| Adult day health care | $95 a day | $24,700 (5 days a week) |
| Assisted living | $6,200 a month | $74,400 |
| Nursing home, shared room | $315 a day | $114,975 |
| Nursing home, private room | $355 a day | $129,575 |

Source: CareScout 2025 Cost of Care Survey [4].

### What these numbers tell you

**Home changes are mostly a one-time cost.** A grab bar, a handrail or better lighting is paid for once. Assisted living and nursing homes are paid every month, year after year.

**Paid help at home adds up fast.** The $80,080 yearly figure assumes about 44 hours of help a week [4]. Many people need far fewer hours, such as a few visits a week for bathing or chores. Others need much more. At full-time levels, in-home help can cost more than assisted living.

**Family time is a real cost too.** Unpaid help from a spouse or adult child does not show up on a bill, but it costs time, energy and sometimes income.

The honest answer is that aging in place is usually the cheaper choice when needs are light to moderate. When someone needs care around the clock, a facility may cost less and be safer.

## What usually needs to change in the home

Most homes were built for younger, able-bodied adults [5]. Common changes include:

- **Bathroom:** grab bars, a non-slip tub or shower floor, a shower seat, a handheld shower head, a taller toilet.
- **Stairs:** sturdy handrails on both sides, bright lights with switches at top and bottom, fixed loose carpet.
- **Entry:** a step-free way in, a ramp or railing, good outdoor lighting.
- **Kitchen:** everyday items moved to waist height, a safe step stool, easy-to-use controls.
- **Bedroom:** a lamp within reach of the bed and night-lights on the path to the bathroom.
- **Whole home:** clear walkways, no throw rugs, lever door handles, working smoke alarms.

Our [home safety checklist](/guides/home-safety-checklist) walks through each room.

## Help beyond the house

A safe home is only half of the plan. Think about:

- **Getting around.** How will you get to the store and the doctor if you stop driving?
- **Daily tasks.** Who can help with cleaning, yard work, meals or bathing if needed?
- **Health care.** Can you get to appointments? Is telehealth an option?
- **Staying connected.** Who will you see each week? Loneliness is a health risk too.
- **Emergencies.** How will you call for help if you fall and cannot reach a phone?

Your local **Area Agency on Aging** can point you to meal programs, rides, in-home help and home repair programs. The fastest way to find yours is the **Eldercare Locator at 1-800-677-1116**, open weekdays from 8 a.m. to 9 p.m. Eastern [6].

## How to pay for changes

There are more ways to pay than most people expect. Options include local grants and nonprofit repair programs, Medicaid waiver programs, VA grants for eligible veterans, USDA repair loans and grants in rural areas, and a tax deduction for some medical home changes. See [how to pay for home modifications](/guides/how-to-pay-for-home-modifications) for the full list.

## Getting started: five first steps

1. **Walk through the home** with our checklist. Write down every problem you see.
2. **Fix the cheap, fast things first.** Lights, rugs, clutter and night-lights cost little and help right away.
3. **Talk to a doctor** about fall risk, medicines and vision.
4. **Get a professional opinion** for bigger changes. An occupational therapist or a Certified Aging-in-Place Specialist can help. See [how to find a CAPS contractor](/guides/find-a-caps-contractor).
5. **Call the Eldercare Locator** to learn what local help and funding you may qualify for [6].

## The bottom line

Aging in place is what most older adults want [2]. It works best with a plan: a safer home, the right help, and a clear view of the costs. Start small, fix the biggest risks first, and get local help early, before a fall or a hospital stay forces fast decisions.

title: Falls at Home: The Facts for Older Adults and What Actually Lowers the Risk
meta_description: Latest CDC data on falls among adults 65+: how common they are, injuries, deaths and costs, plus the steps research shows really cut the risk of falls at home.
short: More than 1 in 4 adults 65 and older fall each year, but research shows targeted home fixes, exercise and a medicine review can cut the risk.

faq.q: How common are falls in older adults?
faq.a: Very common. CDC says more than 1 in 4 adults 65 and older fall each year, which adds up to over 14 million people. Fewer than half tell their doctor.

faq.q: How many older adults die from falls?
faq.a: In 2024, falls caused more than 43,000 deaths among adults 65 and older, according to CDC. Falls are the leading cause of injury death in this age group, and the death rate rose 21% from 2018 to 2024.

faq.q: Do home changes really prevent falls?
faq.a: Yes, for people at higher risk. A 2023 Cochrane review found that home hazard reduction cut the rate of falls by about 38% among people at higher risk, such as those who had fallen in the past year. It showed no clear benefit for people who were not selected for fall risk.

faq.q: If I fall once, am I likely to fall again?
faq.a: Your risk goes up. CDC says one fall doubles the chance of falling again. That is why it is important to tell your doctor about any fall, even one without an injury.

faq.q: What is the single best thing to do after a fall?
faq.a: Tell your doctor and ask for a fall risk check. Then fix the hazards in your home and ask about a strength and balance program. A fall is a warning sign, not just bad luck.

body_md:
Falls are not just a normal part of getting older. They are common, they can be serious, and many of them can be prevented. Here is what the latest CDC data says, and what research shows actually works.

## How common are falls?

**More than 1 in 4 adults age 65 and older fall each year** [1]. That is **over 14 million** older adults reporting a fall [1].

Many falls go unreported. **Fewer than half** of older adults who fall tell their doctor [2]. That matters because one fall is a strong warning. **Falling once doubles the chance of falling again** [2].

## How often do falls cause injuries?

Not every fall causes harm. But many do:

- About **37%** of older adults who fall report an injury that needed medical care or kept them from normal activity for at least a day [2].
- Older adult falls lead to about **4.5 million emergency room visits** a year [2][3].
- Falls lead to about **1.4 million hospital stays** a year [2].
- Nearly **319,000** older adults are hospitalized for a broken hip each year [2].
- Falls caused **88%** of hip fracture ER visits and hospital stays, and **83%** of hip fracture deaths, in 2019 data [2].
- Falls are the **most common cause of traumatic brain injury** in older adults [2].

A broken hip or a head injury can change a person's life. Many people need weeks of rehab. Some never get back to living on their own.

## How many people die from falls?

Falls are the **leading cause of injury death** for adults 65 and older [3]. In 2024, falls caused **more than 43,000 deaths** in this age group [3].

The trend is going the wrong way. The fall death rate for older adults rose **21%**, from **64.7 per 100,000** in 2018 to **78.4 per 100,000** in 2024 [1].

## What do falls cost?

In 2020, U.S. health care spending on **non-fatal** falls among older adults was about **$80 billion** [4]. Most of that was paid by Medicare [4]. That figure does not count lost independence, family caregiving time or the cost of moving to a care setting.

## Where in the home do falls happen?

CDC does not publish a simple room-by-room breakdown of where falls happen. But its home safety checklist points to the same trouble spots again and again [5]:

- **Floors and walkways.** Throw rugs, clutter, cords and furniture in the way.
- **Stairs and steps.** Burned-out bulbs, loose carpet, broken steps, and handrails that are loose or on only one side.
- **Bathrooms.** Slippery tubs and showers, and no grab bars by the tub or toilet.
- **Bedrooms.** A lamp that is hard to reach and a dark path to the bathroom at night.
- **Kitchens.** Items stored up high and wobbly step stools or chairs used to reach them.

These are good places to start your own home check. Our [room-by-room checklist](/guides/home-safety-checklist) covers each one.

## Why older adults fall

Falls usually have more than one cause. Common ones include:

- **Weak legs and poor balance.**
- **Medicines** that cause sleepiness or dizziness, including some you buy without a prescription [5].
- **Vision problems** or out-of-date glasses [5].
- **Getting up too fast** after sitting or lying down, which can cause dizziness [5].
- **Shoes and slippers** that slip or fit poorly, or walking barefoot [5].
- **Home hazards** like the ones listed above.

The more of these that apply, the higher the risk.

## What actually lowers the risk

### 1. Fix home hazards, especially if you are at higher risk

The best evidence on home changes comes from a **2023 Cochrane review**, which pooled many studies [6]. It found:

- Overall, reducing home fall hazards probably cut the **rate of falls by about 26%** [6].
- For people at **higher risk**, the drop was bigger, about **38%** [6]. Higher risk meant people who had fallen in the past year, had been in the hospital recently, or needed help with daily tasks [6].
- For people who were **not chosen because of fall risk**, the review found **no clear benefit** [6].

What this means for you: home changes work best when they are aimed at a real risk. If you or a parent has already fallen, or needs help with daily tasks, fixing the home is one of the best-proven steps you can take. Many of the studies used trained professionals, often occupational therapists, to find and fix hazards [6].

### 2. Build strength and balance

CDC advises exercises that improve leg strength and balance [5]. Many Area Agencies on Aging, senior centers and YMCAs offer group classes. Ask your doctor what is safe for you. You can find your local agency through the Eldercare Locator at 1-800-677-1116 [7].

### 3. Review your medicines

Ask a doctor or pharmacist to go over every medicine you take, including vitamins and over-the-counter pills [5]. Some cause dizziness or drowsiness. Sometimes a dose change or a switch can lower your fall risk.

### 4. Check your eyes

Get an eye exam every year and update your glasses when needed [5].

### 5. Change a few daily habits

- Stand up slowly after sitting or lying down [5].
- Wear shoes with non-slip soles, inside and out [5].
- Keep a phone where you could reach it from the floor [5].
- Consider a device that lets you call for help after a fall [5]. See our guide to [medical alerts and smart home tools](/guides/medical-alert-and-smart-home).

### 6. Talk to your doctor

Tell your doctor about any fall, even a small one. Ask for a fall risk check. CDC also offers a free self-check questionnaire, the **Falls Free CheckUp**, and a planning tool to help you build a prevention plan [3].

## A simple plan for this week

1. **Tonight:** Pick up clutter and cords from walkways. Plug in night-lights between the bed and bathroom.
2. **This week:** Remove or secure throw rugs. Replace burned-out bulbs, especially on stairs.
3. **This month:** Add grab bars in the bathroom and a second stair handrail if you have only one.
4. **At your next checkup:** Ask for a fall risk check, a medicine review and an eye exam referral.

## The bottom line

Falls are common and can be deadly, and the death rate is rising [1][3]. But falls are not a sure thing. The strongest evidence says to **target the people most at risk**, fix the hazards in their homes, and combine that with exercise, a medicine review and good vision care.

title: Home Safety Checklist for Aging in Place: Room by Room
meta_description: A room-by-room home safety checklist for older adults: 100+ checks with the fix and a rough cost tier, based on CDC STEADI, AARP HomeFit and OT guidance.
short: A printable, room-by-room checklist of more than 100 home safety checks, each with a fix and a rough cost tier.

faq.q: Where should I start if I can't fix everything at once?
faq.a: Start with the things linked to the most falls and injuries: clutter and rugs on walkways, lighting on stairs and at night, handrails on both sides of stairs, and grab bars in the bathroom. Many of these are low-cost.

faq.q: What do the $, $$ and $$$ cost tiers mean?
faq.a: They are rough guides, not quotes. $ is a do-it-yourself fix that usually costs little or nothing. $$ usually means buying a product or paying a handyman for a short job. $$$ usually means a contractor, permits or a larger remodel. Local prices vary a lot, so get written bids.

faq.q: Should a professional check the home?
faq.a: If someone has already fallen, has trouble with daily tasks, or has just come home from the hospital, yes. Research shows home changes help most for people at higher risk, and many successful programs used occupational therapists. Medicare Part B may cover an OT home evaluation when it is part of a doctor-ordered therapy plan.

faq.q: Who installs grab bars safely?
faq.a: Grab bars must be anchored into wall studs or with anchors rated for the load. A towel bar is not a grab bar. If you are not sure, hire a licensed handyman or contractor, or ask a local nonprofit repair program.

faq.q: Can I get help paying for these changes?
faq.a: Possibly. Local Area Agencies on Aging, nonprofit repair groups, Medicaid waivers, VA grants and USDA rural repair programs can help, depending on where you live and whether you qualify. Some medical home changes may also count toward the IRS medical expense deduction.

body_md:
Use this checklist to walk through the home one room at a time. Bring a notepad or print this page. Check each item. If the answer points to a problem, write down the fix.

This list draws on CDC's **Check for Safety** home fall checklist [1], the **AARP HomeFit Guide** [2], fire safety advice from the U.S. Fire Administration [4][5], and the kinds of changes occupational therapists (OTs) and Certified Aging-in-Place Specialists recommend [3][7]. The wording and cost tiers are our own.

## How to use this checklist

**Walk it with the person who lives there.** Watch how they actually move. Do they hold onto furniture? Do they step over cords? Do they sit down to dress?

**Check at night, too.** Many problems only show up in the dark.

**Fix in this order:** first the things that could cause a fall today, then the things that make daily tasks hard, then bigger remodels.

### What the cost tiers mean

These are rough guides only, not quotes. Prices vary by region and by home.

- **$** = Do it yourself. Free or low cost (cleaning up, moving items, plug-in night-lights, tape).
- **$$** = A product to buy or a short handyman job (grab bars, handrails, lamps, a shower seat).
- **$$$** = A contractor, electrician or plumber, often with permits (ramps, walk-in showers, new wiring, wider doors).

Always get written bids for $$ and $$$ jobs. See our guide to [home repair scams](/guides/home-repair-scams-seniors) before you hire.

## Why it is worth the effort

Falls caused more than 43,000 deaths among adults 65+ in 2024 [8]. A 2023 Cochrane review found that reducing home hazards cut the rate of falls by about 38% for people at higher risk, such as those who had fallen in the past year [6]. The checklist below is how you find those hazards.

## 1. Entry and front door

- [ ] **Is there a step-free way in, or at least a sturdy railing at the steps?** Add a railing on both sides of entry steps. For a wheelchair or walker user, consider a ramp. *Cost: $$ to $$$*
- [ ] **Is the entry well lit at night?** Install a bright outdoor light, ideally on a motion sensor or timer. *Cost: $$*
- [ ] **Can you see who is at the door without opening it?** Add a peephole at the right height, or a video doorbell. *Cost: $ to $$*
- [ ] **Are the house numbers easy to read from the street at night?** Use large, high-contrast or lighted numbers so emergency crews can find you. *Cost: $*
- [ ] **Is there a place to set bags down while you unlock the door?** Add a small shelf or bench by the door. *Cost: $ to $$*
- [ ] **Is the door threshold raised enough to catch a toe or a walker?** Replace it with a low-profile threshold or add a small threshold ramp. *Cost: $$*
- [ ] **Is the doorknob hard to turn?** Swap round knobs for lever handles. *Cost: $$*
- [ ] **Is the lock hard to use?** Consider a keypad or easy-turn deadbolt. *Cost: $$*
- [ ] **Is the doormat flat and non-slip?** Use a low, rubber-backed mat, or remove it. *Cost: $*
- [ ] **Are the steps even and in good repair?** Fix cracked, loose or uneven steps. *Cost: $$ to $$$*
- [ ] **Is the doorway wide enough for a walker or wheelchair?** Offset ("swing-clear") hinges can add width; a contractor can widen the frame if needed. *Cost: $$ to $$$*

## 2. Stairs and steps

- [ ] **Are there handrails on both sides of the stairs?** Install sturdy handrails on both sides that run the full length of the stairs [1]. *Cost: $$*
- [ ] **Are the handrails solid?** Tighten or replace any rail that wobbles [1]. *Cost: $ to $$*
- [ ] **Is there a light at the top and bottom of the stairs?** Have an electrician add overhead lights [1]. *Cost: $$ to $$$*
- [ ] **Can you turn the stair light on from both the top and the bottom?** Add a switch at each end. Lighted switches help in the dark [1]. *Cost: $$ to $$$*
- [ ] **Are any bulbs burned out?** Replace them right away, and use bright bulbs [1]. *Cost: $*
- [ ] **Is the stair carpet loose or torn?** Fasten it tightly to every step, or remove it and add non-slip treads [1]. *Cost: $ to $$*
- [ ] **Are there things on the stairs?** Keep stairs completely clear [1]. *Cost: $*
- [ ] **Are any steps broken or uneven?** Repair them [1]. *Cost: $$ to $$$*
- [ ] **Can you see the edge of each step?** Mark step edges with a contrasting paint or tape [1]. *Cost: $*
- [ ] **Is climbing the stairs getting hard or unsafe?** Consider moving the bedroom to the main floor, or ask about a stair lift. *Cost: $ (move rooms) to $$$ (stair lift)*

## 3. Living room and hallways

- [ ] **Do you have to walk around furniture to cross the room?** Move furniture to create clear, wide paths [1]. *Cost: $*
- [ ] **Are there throw rugs?** Remove them, or secure them with double-sided tape or a non-slip backing [1]. *Cost: $*
- [ ] **Are papers, shoes, books or blankets on the floor?** Pick them up and keep floors clear [1]. *Cost: $*
- [ ] **Do cords run across walkways?** Run them along the wall. Have an electrician add an outlet if needed [1]. *Cost: $ to $$*
- [ ] **Is the favorite chair easy to get out of?** Chairs with firm seats and armrests are easier. Furniture risers can raise a low seat. *Cost: $ to $$*
- [ ] **Can you reach a light switch when you walk into the room?** Add a lamp on a smart plug, a plug-in switch, or a new switch by the door. *Cost: $ to $$$*
- [ ] **Is the floor slippery or uneven?** Fix loose boards or tiles, and skip high-gloss floor wax. *Cost: $ to $$$*
- [ ] **Do pets sleep in walkways or run underfoot?** Give pets a bed out of the main path and know where they are before you stand. *Cost: $*
- [ ] **Is there a phone you can reach from a chair?** Keep a phone, or a cell phone, within easy reach. *Cost: $*
- [ ] **Are hallways bright enough?** Add brighter bulbs or plug-in lights, and light dark corners [1]. *Cost: $*
- [ ] **Is there glare from windows or shiny floors?** Use light curtains or shades to soften glare [1]. *Cost: $ to $$*
- [ ] **Is the thermostat easy to read and reach?** Consider a large-display or programmable model. *Cost: $$*

## 4. Kitchen

- [ ] **Are the things you use most kept up high?** Move them to shelves between about waist and shoulder height [1]. *Cost: $*
- [ ] **Do you use a chair to reach things?** Never stand on a chair. Use a sturdy step stool with a handle bar [1]. *Cost: $$*
- [ ] **Do you stay in the kitchen while the stove is on?** Cooking is the leading cause of home fires and home fire injuries. Unattended equipment is the top factor in kitchen fires that spread [5]. Use a timer as a reminder [4]. *Cost: $*
- [ ] **Is there a pan lid or baking sheet nearby?** Keep one handy to smother a small pan fire [5]. *Cost: $*
- [ ] **Are towels, mitts or paper near the burners?** Keep anything that can burn away from the stovetop [5]. *Cost: $*
- [ ] **Do pot handles point outward?** Turn handles toward the back of the stove [5]. *Cost: $*
- [ ] **Are appliances plugged into extension cords?** Plug them straight into the wall [5]. *Cost: $*
- [ ] **Are stove knobs easy to read and turn?** Add large, high-contrast labels. For memory concerns, ask about an automatic stove shutoff device. *Cost: $ to $$*
- [ ] **Is the floor slippery near the sink?** Wipe spills right away and use a low, non-slip mat. *Cost: $*
- [ ] **Is there good light over the counter and sink?** Add under-cabinet lights. *Cost: $$*
- [ ] **Are cabinet knobs hard to grip?** Swap them for D-shaped pulls. *Cost: $ to $$*
- [ ] **Are heavy pots stored low and deep?** Use pull-out shelves or store heavy items at counter height. *Cost: $$ to $$$*
- [ ] **Is there a place to sit while prepping food?** A stool or chair at counter height can help with fatigue. *Cost: $$*

## 5. Bedroom

- [ ] **Can you turn on a light without getting out of bed?** Place a lamp within easy reach of the bed [1]. *Cost: $*
- [ ] **Is the path from the bed to the bathroom dark?** Add night-lights. Some turn on by themselves when it gets dark [1]. *Cost: $*
- [ ] **Is the bed the right height?** Your feet should rest flat on the floor when you sit on the edge. Adjust with risers or a different frame. *Cost: $ to $$*
- [ ] **Is there something sturdy to hold onto when getting out of bed?** Ask an OT about a bed rail or support handle that is safe for you. *Cost: $$*
- [ ] **Is there clutter or a rug between the bed and the door?** Keep the path clear and rug-free [1]. *Cost: $*
- [ ] **Is there a phone near the bed?** Keep one within reach, plus a list of emergency numbers [1]. *Cost: $*
- [ ] **Are clothes easy to reach?** Lower closet rods and move daily items to middle drawers. *Cost: $ to $$*
- [ ] **Is there a chair to sit on while dressing?** Use a firm chair with arms. *Cost: $ to $$*
- [ ] **Is there a working smoke alarm in or near the bedroom?** Test it monthly. If you cannot hear it, use an alarm with a bed shaker or strobe light [4]. *Cost: $ to $$*
- [ ] **Is there a flashlight by the bed for power outages?** Keep one with fresh batteries. *Cost: $*

## 6. Bathroom

- [ ] **Is the tub or shower floor slippery?** Add a non-slip mat or self-stick strips [1]. *Cost: $*
- [ ] **Are there grab bars in and next to the tub or shower?** Install grab bars anchored into studs [1]. Never use a towel bar or soap dish for support. *Cost: $$*
- [ ] **Is there a grab bar next to the toilet?** Install one, or use a sturdy toilet safety frame [1]. *Cost: $$*
- [ ] **Is the toilet hard to get up from?** Add a raised seat, or replace it with a taller ("comfort height") toilet. *Cost: $$ to $$$*
- [ ] **Is stepping over the tub wall hard?** Use a tub transfer bench, or consider a walk-in or curbless shower. *Cost: $$ to $$$*
- [ ] **Is there a seat in the shower?** Add a shower chair or bench. *Cost: $$*
- [ ] **Is there a handheld shower head?** It lets you wash while seated. *Cost: $ to $$*
- [ ] **Is the water too hot?** Set the water heater to about 120°F or add anti-scald valves. *Cost: $ to $$*
- [ ] **Is the bath mat outside the tub non-slip?** Use one with a rubber backing, or remove it. *Cost: $*
- [ ] **Is there a night-light?** Add one so the bathroom is never fully dark. *Cost: $*
- [ ] **Do faucets use round knobs?** Lever or single-handle faucets are easier for stiff hands. *Cost: $$*
- [ ] **Does the door open outward or slide?** A door that swings in can block help from getting to someone who has fallen. A contractor can rehang it or install a pocket or barn door. *Cost: $$ to $$$*
- [ ] **Can the bathroom door be unlocked from outside in an emergency?** Use a privacy lock that can be opened from the hall. *Cost: $*
- [ ] **Are toiletries easy to reach without bending or stretching?** Add a shower caddy or a shelf at shoulder height. *Cost: $*

## 7. Laundry area

- [ ] **Are the washer and dryer in the basement or up a flight of stairs?** Consider moving laundry to the main floor if stairs are hard. *Cost: $$$*
- [ ] **Is the path to the laundry clear and well lit?** Clear it and add lighting. *Cost: $ to $$*
- [ ] **Do you carry heavy baskets on stairs?** Use smaller loads, a bag with a shoulder strap, or a rolling cart on the same floor. *Cost: $*
- [ ] **Are the machines easy to load?** Pedestals can raise front-loaders to reduce bending. *Cost: $$*
- [ ] **Are detergent and supplies at waist height?** Move them to a shelf you can reach without a stool. *Cost: $*
- [ ] **Is the floor slippery from spills or leaks?** Clean spills and fix leaks. *Cost: $ to $$*
- [ ] **Is the dryer lint filter cleaned after every load?** Clean it each time, and have the vent cleaned regularly. *Cost: $ to $$*
- [ ] **Is there a place to sit while folding?** Fold at a table or counter with a chair nearby. *Cost: $*

## 8. Outdoors, garage and yard

- [ ] **Are walkways even and free of cracks or tree roots?** Repair or patch trip hazards. *Cost: $$ to $$$*
- [ ] **Are paths lit from the car to the door?** Add path lights or motion-sensor lights. *Cost: $$*
- [ ] **Are outdoor steps marked and railed?** Paint edges a contrasting color and add railings [1]. *Cost: $ to $$*
- [ ] **Is there a plan for snow, ice and wet leaves?** Arrange shoveling and use salt or sand. Ask about local chore programs. *Cost: $ to $$*
- [ ] **Are hoses, tools and toys put away?** Keep paths clear. *Cost: $*
- [ ] **Is the garage floor clear and well lit?** Clear clutter and add bright lights. *Cost: $ to $$*
- [ ] **Is the step from the garage into the house safe?** Add a railing or a short ramp. *Cost: $$ to $$$*
- [ ] **Is the mailbox easy and safe to reach?** Consider a mailbox closer to the door, if allowed. *Cost: $$*
- [ ] **Are gutters cleaned by someone else?** Older adults should not climb ladders. Hire help or ask a volunteer program. *Cost: $$*
- [ ] **Is the deck or porch in good shape?** Fix soft or loose boards and loose railings. *Cost: $$ to $$$*

## 9. Lighting (whole home)

- [ ] **Is the lighting bright and even, with no dark spots?** Use brighter bulbs and add light to dark areas [1]. *Cost: $*
- [ ] **Is there a light switch at every room entrance?** Add switches or remote-control or smart plugs. *Cost: $ to $$$*
- [ ] **Are there night-lights in halls, the bedroom and the bathroom?** Use plug-in or motion-sensor night-lights [1]. *Cost: $*
- [ ] **Do lamps have cords that cross walkways?** Re-route them along walls [1]. *Cost: $*
- [ ] **Is there harsh glare?** Use shades, frosted bulbs or indirect lighting [1]. *Cost: $ to $$*
- [ ] **Are closets dark?** Add battery or plug-in closet lights. *Cost: $*
- [ ] **Are light switches easy to see in the dark?** Use lighted or glow switches [1]. *Cost: $ to $$*
- [ ] **Is there light at the top and bottom of every staircase?** See the stairs section above [1]. *Cost: $$ to $$$*
- [ ] **Do you have flashlights in key rooms?** Keep one in the bedroom, kitchen and living room. *Cost: $*

## 10. Emergency readiness

- [ ] **Are emergency numbers posted in large print near each phone?** Post them where they are easy to see [1]. *Cost: $*
- [ ] **Could you reach a phone if you fell?** Keep a phone low enough to reach from the floor, or carry a cell phone [1]. *Cost: $*
- [ ] **Do you have a way to call for help if you cannot get up?** Consider a medical alert device [1]. See our [medical alert guide](/guides/medical-alert-and-smart-home). *Cost: $$*
- [ ] **Are smoke alarms on every level and near sleeping areas, and do they work?** Test monthly. Use bed-shaker or strobe alarms if hearing is limited [4]. *Cost: $ to $$*
- [ ] **Do you have carbon monoxide alarms if you have gas appliances or an attached garage?** Install them and test them. *Cost: $ to $$*
- [ ] **Do you have a fire escape plan?** Plan your route with family and neighbors. Make sure a walker or wheelchair fits through each exit door [4]. *Cost: $*
- [ ] **If you use medical oxygen, does anyone smoke nearby?** Never smoke near oxygen [4]. *Cost: $*
- [ ] **Is there a fire extinguisher in the kitchen that you know how to use?** Keep one and learn how to use it. *Cost: $$*
- [ ] **Does someone check on you every day?** Set up a daily call or text with family, a friend or a check-in program. *Cost: $*
- [ ] **Is there a current list of medicines, doctors and contacts?** Keep it on the fridge or by the door for emergency crews. *Cost: $*
- [ ] **Does a trusted neighbor have a spare key, or is there a lockbox?** This lets help get in without breaking a door. *Cost: $ to $$*
- [ ] **Do you have supplies for a power outage or storm?** Keep water, food, medicines and batteries for a few days. *Cost: $ to $$*

## Daily habits that go with a safe home

A safer house works best with a few habits [1]:

- Have a doctor or pharmacist review all your medicines.
- Get your eyes checked every year.
- Stand up slowly after sitting or lying down.
- Wear shoes with non-slip soles inside and outside. Avoid going barefoot or wearing loose slippers.
- Do exercises that build leg strength and balance.

## When to bring in a professional

Call in help if:

- Someone has **already fallen** or is afraid of falling.
- Someone has **trouble with daily tasks** like bathing, toileting or dressing.
- Someone just came **home from the hospital** or rehab.
- The fix needs **wiring, plumbing, permits or structural work**.

An **occupational therapist** can look at how a person moves and suggest changes that fit them. Medicare Part B may cover an OT home evaluation when it is part of a medically needed therapy plan ordered after an illness or injury. A purely preventive visit is usually not covered [7]. A **Certified Aging-in-Place Specialist (CAPS)** is a remodeler or other pro trained by the National Association of Home Builders in aging-in-place design [3]. See [how to find a CAPS contractor](/guides/find-a-caps-contractor).

## Next steps

1. Mark every "no" on this list.
2. Do all the **$** fixes this week.
3. Get bids for the **$$** and **$$$** items, starting with stairs and the bathroom.
4. Read [how to pay for home modifications](/guides/how-to-pay-for-home-modifications) to see what help you might qualify for.

title: How to Pay for Home Modifications: Every Option for Older Adults
meta_description: Grants, loans, Medicaid waivers, VA grants, USDA repair help, tax deductions, reverse mortgages and nonprofits: every way to pay for aging-in-place changes.
short: An overview of every main way to pay for grab bars, ramps, walk-in showers and other aging-in-place changes, and who to call first.

faq.q: Is there a government grant for seniors to fix their homes?
faq.a: There is no single national grant that everyone can get. Instead, there are many smaller programs. The main federal one with a set grant is USDA's Section 504 program, which offers grants of up to $10,000 to very-low-income homeowners 62 and older in eligible rural areas. Others are run by states, counties, cities and nonprofits.

faq.q: Does Medicare pay for grab bars or a walk-in shower?
faq.a: Original Medicare generally does not pay for home modifications. It may cover an occupational therapy home evaluation when it is part of a doctor-ordered therapy plan. Some Medicare Advantage plans offer extra benefits, so check your plan's coverage documents.

faq.q: Who should I call first?
faq.a: Call the Eldercare Locator at 1-800-677-1116 to reach your local Area Agency on Aging. They know which repair grants, Medicaid waiver programs and nonprofit programs operate where you live.

faq.q: Can I deduct home modifications on my taxes?
faq.a: Possibly. IRS Publication 502 lets you count some home changes made for medical care, such as ramps, grab bars and wider doorways, as medical expenses. You only benefit if you itemize and your total medical costs exceed 7.5% of your adjusted gross income.

faq.q: Should I use a reverse mortgage to pay for changes?
faq.a: It is one option for homeowners 62 and older, but it is a loan with fees and rules, and you must keep paying taxes and insurance. HUD requires counseling with an approved counselor first. Look at grants and lower-cost options before borrowing against your home.

faq.q: Will anyone charge me to apply for a home repair grant?
faq.a: Real government grants do not charge an application fee. If someone calls to say you won a grant, or asks for a fee or your bank details, it is a scam.

body_md:
Grab bars, ramps, a walk-in shower or a stair lift can make the difference between staying home and having to move. But who pays? The good news is that there are many sources of help. The hard part is that most are local, have waiting lists, and have their own rules.

This guide gives you the full map. Each section explains one type of help, who it is for, and where to start.

## Start here: call your Area Agency on Aging

Before you do anything else, call the **Eldercare Locator at 1-800-677-1116** [1]. It is a free federal service. Specialists answer **Monday through Friday, 8 a.m. to 9 p.m. Eastern** [1]. They will connect you to your local **Area Agency on Aging (AAA)**.

Your AAA is the best single place to ask, "What help is there for home repairs and changes where I live?" Many AAAs use federal Older Americans Act funds for small home repair and modification programs, and they keep track of other local programs too. Ask about waiting lists, income limits and what the program covers.

TTY users can dial 711 and ask for 1-800-677-1116 [1].

## 1. Local grants and nonprofit repair programs

**What it is:** Free or low-cost repairs done by a nonprofit or a city or county program.

**Examples:**
- **Rebuilding Together.** Its *Safe at Home* program offers free home changes for older adults and people with disabilities. Work can include grab bars, handrails, ramps, wider doors, tub and shower changes, raised toilets, smoke and CO alarms, and better lighting [2]. You apply through your local affiliate [2].
- **Habitat for Humanity** affiliates and other local repair groups often run home repair programs for older homeowners.
- **City and county programs** often use federal housing money, such as HUD's Community Development Block Grant (CDBG), which also helps fund some local nonprofit repair work [2]. Some use HUD HOME program funds. Ask your city or county housing office.

**Who it is for:** Usually homeowners with low or moderate incomes. Rules differ by program.

**Tip:** Funds often run out early in the year. Apply as soon as you can and ask to be put on the waiting list.

## 2. USDA Section 504 rural repair loans and grants

**What it is:** Help from USDA Rural Development for very-low-income homeowners in eligible rural areas [3].

**Key facts** [3]:
- **Grants** of up to **$10,000** (a lifetime limit) to remove health and safety hazards. You must be **62 or older**.
- **Loans** of up to **$40,000** at a fixed **1%** interest rate for up to **20 years**, to repair, improve or update the home.
- You can combine a loan and grant for up to **$50,000**.
- You must own and live in the home, be unable to get affordable credit elsewhere, and meet the income limit for your county.
- A grant may have to be paid back if you sell the home within 3 years.

**Where to start:** Your local USDA Rural Development office.

## 3. Medicaid waiver programs

**What it is:** Most states run Medicaid **home and community-based services (HCBS) waivers**. These programs help people who would otherwise qualify for nursing home care to get care at home instead [4]. Nearly every state and D.C. offers them [4].

**How it helps:** States design their own waivers and choose the services [4]. Many state waivers for older adults or people with disabilities include home accessibility changes, such as ramps or grab bars, along with in-home care. Program names vary by state.

**Who it is for:** People who meet Medicaid's income and asset limits *and* need a nursing-home level of care. Many waivers have caps on how many people they serve, so waiting lists are common [4].

**Where to start:** Your AAA or your state Medicaid agency.

## 4. Medicare and Medicare Advantage

**Original Medicare** generally does not pay for home modifications like grab bars or ramps.

It **may** pay for an **occupational therapy (OT) home evaluation** when the visit is part of a skilled therapy plan, for example after an illness or injury [5]. A purely preventive "aging in place" evaluation is usually not covered [5].

**Medicare Advantage plans** sometimes offer extra benefits, such as bathroom safety items. Coverage varies by plan and year. Check your plan's *Evidence of Coverage* or call the plan.

## 5. VA grants for veterans

The Department of Veterans Affairs offers housing grants for veterans with certain service-connected disabilities. For fiscal year 2026, the maximum amounts are [6]:

- **Specially Adapted Housing (SAH):** up to **$126,526**
- **Special Home Adaptation (SHA):** up to **$25,350**
- **Temporary Residence Adaptation (TRA):** up to **$50,961** for those who qualify for SAH, or **$9,100** for those who qualify for SHA

VA health care also has a separate, smaller **Home Improvements and Structural Alterations (HISA)** grant for medically needed changes. Ask your VA health care team about it.

**Where to start:** VA.gov or your local VA medical center. A county Veterans Service Officer can help you apply for free.

## 6. Tax deduction for medical home changes

**What it is:** The IRS lets you count some home changes made for medical reasons as **medical expenses** [7].

**What can count** [7]: ramps, wider doorways and hallways, railings and grab bars, lowered kitchen cabinets, moved outlets and switches, porch lifts, modified stairways, changes to door hardware, and grading the ground to make the home reachable.

**Key rules** [7]:
- If a change does not raise your home's value, the whole cost can count.
- If it does raise the value, only the cost above the increase in value counts.
- Only reasonable costs count, not extras for looks.
- You must **itemize**, and you can only deduct the part of your total medical costs above **7.5% of your adjusted gross income**.

Keep receipts and a note from your doctor. Talk to a tax preparer. Some states also offer their own tax credits for accessibility changes.

## 7. Reverse mortgage (HECM)

**What it is:** A **Home Equity Conversion Mortgage (HECM)** is a federally insured reverse mortgage. It lets homeowners turn part of their home equity into cash without monthly mortgage payments [8].

**Key rules** [8]:
- You must be **62 or older**, own the home outright or have a lot of equity, and live there as your main home.
- You must meet with a **HUD-approved counselor** first. You can find one by calling **(800) 569-4287**.
- You must keep paying property taxes, insurance and HOA fees.
- Closing costs and fees can be paid from the loan, which lowers what you get.

**Be careful:** A reverse mortgage is a loan, not a grant. It reduces what you or your heirs get from the home later. Look at grants first. Never let a contractor push you into a reverse mortgage or home equity loan to pay *them* [9].

## 8. Other loans

- **FHA 203(k) loans** let buyers or owners roll repair costs into an FHA mortgage.
- **State housing finance agencies** in some states offer low-interest or deferred loans for repairs and accessibility.
- **State assistive technology programs** often run low-interest loan funds for equipment such as stair lifts and ramps, and many lend or recycle equipment for free.
- **Home equity loans or lines of credit** are another option, but compare terms carefully.

## 9. Other helpers worth a call

- **Centers for Independent Living** help people with disabilities of all ages, including with home access.
- **State vocational rehabilitation** may help if home changes are needed to keep working.
- **The Weatherization Assistance Program** pays for energy repairs, which sometimes frees up other money for safety changes.

## 10. Family and payment plans

Many families split the cost. Tips:

- **Agree in writing** who pays what, and whether money is a gift or a loan.
- **Fix the biggest risks first** so a small budget does the most good.
- **Never pay in full up front.** The FTC warns against paying the whole amount before work begins and against making the last payment until the job is done right [9].
- **Compare any contractor financing** with other loan options before you sign [9].

## Watch out for grant scams

Real government grants **never charge an application fee** [10]. Federal grants require an application; no one can award you a grant over the phone [10]. If a caller says you "qualify for a free government grant" and asks for a fee or your bank account number, hang up. Report it to the FTC at 1-877-382-4357 [10].

## A simple plan

1. **Call the Eldercare Locator** (1-800-677-1116) and ask your AAA what programs fit you [1].
2. **List the changes you need** using our [home safety checklist](/guides/home-safety-checklist).
3. **Apply to every program you might qualify for.** Many people combine two or three sources.
4. **Get written bids** from licensed, insured contractors. See [how to find a CAPS contractor](/guides/find-a-caps-contractor).
5. **Keep every receipt** for possible tax deductions [7].

short: How to find and vet a Certified Aging-in-Place Specialist, and when to bring in an occupational therapist first.

faq.q: What does CAPS stand for?
faq.a: CAPS means Certified Aging-in-Place Specialist. It is a credential from the National Association of Home Builders (NAHB) for remodelers, builders, occupational therapists and others who help make homes work for people as they age.

faq.q: Is a CAPS credential the same as a contractor's license?
faq.a: No. CAPS shows training in aging-in-place design. It does not replace a state or local contractor license. Always check the license and insurance separately.

faq.q: Where is the official CAPS directory?
faq.a: NAHB lists credential holders in its 'Professionals with Home Building Credentials' directory, found on the NAHB Directories page at nahb.org. You can also call NAHB at 800-368-5242 to ask about a designee.

faq.q: Should I hire an occupational therapist before a contractor?
faq.a: If the person has fallen, has a health condition that affects movement, or just left the hospital, an OT home assessment first is a smart move. The OT looks at how the person moves and what they need. The contractor then builds it.

faq.q: Will Medicare pay for an occupational therapy home assessment?
faq.a: Medicare Part B may cover an OT home evaluation when it is part of a medically needed therapy plan, such as after an illness. A purely preventive assessment is usually not covered, and the therapist may ask you to sign a notice that you will pay.

body_md:
Putting in a grab bar is not hard. Putting it in the *right place*, anchored the *right way*, for the *person who will use it* takes more skill. That is where a **Certified Aging-in-Place Specialist (CAPS)** and an **occupational therapist (OT)** can help.

## What is a CAPS?

**CAPS** is a credential from the **National Association of Home Builders (NAHB)** [1][2]. It is for people who plan and build home changes that help older adults stay in their homes. CAPS holders include remodelers, builders, contractors and occupational therapists [1][2]. Some designers and other pros earn it too.

### What CAPS holders must do

To earn the credential, a person must [1]:

- Complete **three courses**:
  - CAPS I: Marketing and Communicating with the Aging-in-Place Client
  - CAPS II: Design Concepts and Methods for Livable Homes and Aging in Place
  - CAPS III: Details and Solutions for Livable Homes and Aging in Place
- Sign the **CAPS code of ethics** pledge.
- If they are a remodeler or contractor, show proof of **liability and workers' compensation insurance** where required, and a **business license** if their state requires one.

To keep it, they must take **continuing education** (four hours a year) and **renew every year** [1].

### What CAPS does *not* mean

CAPS is **training**, not a license. It does not prove the person is licensed to do construction in your state. It is also not a guarantee of good work. Use it as a starting point, then check the person out like you would any contractor.

## How to find a CAPS professional

### Use the official NAHB directory

NAHB keeps a directory called **"Professionals with Home Building Credentials."** NAHB says these members hold credentials in specialties such as **CAPS** [2]. You can reach it from the **NAHB Directories** page at nahb.org [2].

If someone says they are CAPS-certified and you cannot find them, ask for their NAHB designee information. Then call NAHB's education line at **(800) 368-5242** to check [1].

### Other ways to find one

- **Ask your Area Agency on Aging.** Call the Eldercare Locator at 1-800-677-1116 [6].
- **Ask an occupational therapist** or your doctor's office for names they trust.
- **Ask your local home builders association.** The FTC also suggests checking with them for complaints [5].
- **Ask nonprofit repair programs.** Some work with OTs and local contractors (see below).

Try to get **at least three names**, and get written bids from more than one.

## Questions to ask before you hire

Ask every contractor, CAPS or not:

1. **Are you licensed in this state? What is your license number?** Then check it yourself with your state or county [5].
2. **Can you show proof of liability and workers' compensation insurance?** [5]
3. **Are you CAPS-certified? Since when?** Check the NAHB directory [2].
4. **How many aging-in-place projects have you done? Can I call two or three of those clients?**
5. **Will you work with our occupational therapist, or do you have one you work with?**
6. **Who will pull the permits?** The contractor should. The FTC warns that asking *you* to get permits is a red flag [5].
7. **What exactly is included in the price?** Get a written, itemized estimate.
8. **What is the schedule?** The contract should list start and finish dates [5].
9. **How do payments work?** Never pay the full amount up front. Some states limit down payments [5].
10. **What warranty do you offer on work and products?**
11. **How will you anchor grab bars?** They must go into studs or use anchors rated for the weight. A towel bar is not a grab bar.
12. **Do you design to the person's needs, or use a standard package?** Good aging-in-place work is fitted to the person. Ask about heights, sides of the toilet, and walker or wheelchair space.

## Red flags

Walk away if a contractor [5]:

- Knocks on your door saying they are "in the area" or have leftover materials.
- Pushes you to decide **today**.
- Wants **full payment up front** or **cash only**.
- Asks **you** to get the building permits.
- Suggests you borrow from **a lender they know**.
- Gives a vague contract with **blank spaces** or makes promises that are not in writing.

Also be wary of any "free safety inspection" that turns into a big, urgent sales pitch. See our full guide to [home repair scams](/guides/home-repair-scams-seniors).

## Before you sign

Make sure the contract includes [5]:

- The contractor's name, address, phone and **license number**.
- A detailed list of work and materials.
- **Start and finish dates.**
- The payment schedule.
- Any promises made out loud, now in writing.
- No blank spaces.

If you sign at home, you may have **three business days to cancel** under the FTC's Cooling-Off Rule. Some exceptions apply, such as repairs you asked for or true emergencies [8].

## Occupational therapy home assessments

### What an OT does

An **occupational therapist** looks at how a person actually lives in the home. They watch the person get in and out of the tub, use the toilet, climb stairs, cook and get out of bed. Then they suggest changes and equipment that fit that person's body, health and goals.

An OT may suggest things a contractor would not think of, like which side to put a grab bar on, or whether a tub bench will work better than a full remodel. That can save money.

### When to get one first

An OT assessment is a good first step when:

- Someone has **already fallen** or is afraid of falling.
- Someone has a condition that affects movement, balance, vision or memory.
- Someone is coming **home from a hospital or rehab**.
- You are planning a **big project**, like a bathroom remodel or ramp.

Research backs this up. A 2023 Cochrane review found that reducing home hazards cut falls by about **38%** for people at higher risk. Many of the studies used OTs or other trained professionals to find and fix hazards [3].

### Does Medicare pay for it?

Sometimes. **Medicare Part B** may cover an OT home evaluation when it is part of a **medically needed therapy plan**, for example after a health problem that caused a decline [4]. A purely **preventive** aging-in-place assessment is usually **not** covered. In that case, the OT may ask you to sign a notice saying you will pay yourself [4]. If a home builder hires the OT, Medicare is not billed [4].

Ask your doctor for a referral if you think the visit may qualify.

### OTs and nonprofit programs

Some nonprofit repair programs pair OTs with contractors. For example, HUD's Older Adult Home Modification Program grants given to Rebuilding Together required a home assessment by a licensed OT before work began [7]. Ask local programs whether they include an OT visit.

## Putting it together

1. **Get an OT assessment** if there is a health or fall concern.
2. **Find two or three CAPS pros** in the NAHB directory, or through your AAA [2][6].
3. **Check licenses and insurance** yourself [5].
4. **Get written, itemized bids** and compare them.
5. **Sign a clear contract** and never pay everything up front [5].
6. **Look for funding** before you start. See [how to pay for home modifications](/guides/how-to-pay-for-home-modifications).

title: Home Repair Scams That Target Older Homeowners, and How to Stop Them
meta_description: Door-to-door contractors, storm chasers, fake grants and loan traps: how home repair scams target older adults, the warning signs, and how to protect yourself.
short: The most common home repair and fake-grant scams aimed at older homeowners, the warning signs, and what to do if you are targeted.

faq.q: What is the most common home repair scam?
faq.a: A contractor shows up uninvited, says they are working nearby or have leftover materials, points out an 'urgent' problem, and pushes you to pay up front. They then do poor work or none at all.

faq.q: How much deposit should I pay a contractor?
faq.a: Never pay the full amount up front. AARP advises paying no more than one-third of the estimate as a deposit, and some states set their own limits. Make the final payment only after the work is done and you are satisfied.

faq.q: Can I cancel a contract I signed at my kitchen table?
faq.a: Often, yes. Under the FTC's Cooling-Off Rule, you usually have until midnight of the third business day to cancel many sales made in your home, if the sale is $25 or more. Repairs you asked for and true emergencies are exceptions.

faq.q: Someone called to say I qualify for a free home repair grant. Is it real?
faq.a: Almost certainly not. Real government grants require an application and never charge a fee. Grants are not given by phone or by drawing. Hang up and report it to the FTC.

faq.q: Where do I report a home repair scam?
faq.a: Report it to your state attorney general or local consumer protection office, and to the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov. If money was lost, also call your local police. AARP's Fraud Watch Network helpline is 877-908-3360.

body_md:
Most contractors are honest. But home repair is also one of the most common ways scammers go after older homeowners. They know many older adults own their homes, may be home during the day, and may feel pressure to fix a problem fast.

The stakes are high. In 2024, people over 60 filed **147,127 complaints** with the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center and reported about **$4.9 billion** in losses, up 43% from the year before [1]. Those figures cover all online fraud, not just home repair, but they show how often older adults are targeted.

## The most common home repair scams

### 1. The "we're working in the area" knock

Someone knocks and says they are working on a nearby house. They noticed a problem with your roof, driveway or gutters. They have **leftover materials** and can give you a great deal if you decide **now** [2][3]. Once paid, they do a poor job, or vanish.

### 2. The storm chaser

After a storm, crews show up offering fast repairs or cleanup. Some ask for money before they start or ask you to **sign over your insurance check** [3][4]. Some take the money and leave. Others do shoddy work at high prices [4].

### 3. The costly "free inspection"

A worker offers a free check of your roof, furnace or foundation. They "find" a serious problem that is small or not there at all, then push for an expensive fix right away [3].

### 4. The upfront payment trap

The contractor wants a large deposit, the **full price up front**, or **cash only** [2][3]. Some ask for gift cards, wire transfers or cryptocurrency, which are hard to trace or get back [3].

### 5. The loan or deed trap

The contractor offers to "help" you pay by setting up a loan through a lender they know [2]. Some push a home equity loan or reverse mortgage that pays *them* directly [4]. The terms can be awful. In the worst cases, people are tricked into signing papers that put their home at risk. The FTC warns never to sign over your deed without talking to a lawyer or someone you trust [2].

### 6. Fake government grant calls

A caller, email or social media message says you qualify for a **free government grant** for home repairs. You just need to pay a "processing fee" or share your bank account number [5][6]. This is a scam. Federal grants have no application fee, require a real application, and are never awarded by drawing or over the phone [5].

### 7. Impostors at the door

Some people pretend to be from the **utility company** or the **city** and say they must come in to check something. Ask for ID, then call the utility or city at the number on your bill or on its official website before you let anyone in.

## Warning signs: stop if you hear these

- "I'm working in the neighborhood and have materials left over." [2]
- "This price is only good today." [2]
- "I need the full amount up front," or "Cash only." [2]
- "You'll need to get the permits yourself." [2]
- "I know a lender who can finance this for you." [2]
- "Just sign here, we'll fill in the rest later." [2]
- "Sign your insurance check over to me." [3]
- "You've won a free government grant." [5]

## How to protect yourself

### Before you hire

- **Don't hire from a knock on the door.** Find contractors yourself [4].
- **Get recommendations** from people you trust [2].
- **Check the license** with your state or county, and ask for **proof of insurance** [2].
- **Look for complaints** with your state attorney general, local consumer protection office and local home builders association. Search the company name online with words like "scam" or "complaint" [2].
- **Get at least two or three written bids.** Don't just take the lowest. Ask why bids are far apart [2].

### The contract

Get everything in writing. A good contract lists [2]:

- The contractor's name, address, phone and **license number**.
- The work to be done and the materials.
- **Start and finish dates.**
- The payment schedule.
- Any spoken promises.

Don't sign anything with **blank spaces**, anything you haven't read, or anything in a language you don't fully understand [2].

### Paying

- **Never pay the full amount up front** [2]. Some states limit how much a contractor can ask for as a down payment [2].
- AARP advises a deposit of **no more than one-third** of the estimate [3].
- **Pay by check or credit card**, not cash [4].
- **Make the final payment only when the work is done** and you are happy with it [2].
- **Don't accept contractor financing** until you have compared it with other loans and know you can afford it [2].

### Your right to cancel

The FTC's **Cooling-Off Rule** gives you until **midnight of the third business day** to cancel many sales made at your home that cost **$25 or more**, or $130 or more at a temporary location like a fair or hotel room [7]. Saturdays count as business days; Sundays and federal holidays do not [7].

To cancel, sign and date the cancellation form and mail it, or write a letter. Use **certified mail** and keep a copy [7]. You don't have to give a reason [7]. The seller must refund your money within 10 days [7].

**Know the exceptions** [7]: the rule does not cover repairs or maintenance **you asked for** (though extra items they sell you while there may be covered), or sales needed to meet a true **emergency**. Some states give you more rights than the federal rule.

## Protecting a parent

Adult children can help a lot:

- **Agree on a rule:** no work gets hired without a call to a family member first.
- **Post a "No Soliciting" sign** and a note by the door: "I don't buy at the door."
- **Be the second set of eyes** on any contract or bid.
- **Watch the bank account** if your parent agrees, so odd payments get caught fast.
- **Know the signs of memory problems.** Scammers target people who are confused or forgetful [4].

## If you think you've been scammed

1. **Stop paying.** Contact your bank or card company right away.
2. **Write everything down:** names, dates, phone numbers, plate numbers, receipts.
3. **Try the contractor first in writing.** Follow up any call with a letter by certified mail, return receipt requested [2].
4. **Report it** to your **state attorney general** or local consumer protection office [2], and to the **FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov** or 1-877-382-4357 [2][5].
5. **Call the police** if money was taken and no work was done.
6. **Get support.** AARP's Fraud Watch Network helpline is **877-908-3360** [3].

Being scammed is not your fault. Reporting it helps stop the same person from hitting your neighbors.

## Where to find honest help

- Your **Area Agency on Aging** can point you to vetted repair programs. Call the Eldercare Locator at 1-800-677-1116.
- **Nonprofit repair programs** like Rebuilding Together do free work for eligible older adults.
- Learn how to vet pros in our guide to [finding a CAPS contractor](/guides/find-a-caps-contractor), and see real funding options in [how to pay for home modifications](/guides/how-to-pay-for-home-modifications).

title: Medical Alerts and Smart Home Tech for Aging in Place: What Helps and What It Costs
meta_description: Medical alert systems, fall detection, smart lights, video doorbells and stove shutoffs: what really helps older adults at home, typical costs and privacy tips.
short: A no-brand guide to medical alert systems, fall detection and smart home tools for older adults, with typical costs and privacy tips.

faq.q: How much does a medical alert system cost?
faq.a: A 2025 NCOA review found monthly fees from about $19.95 to $159.95, before fall detection. Fall detection usually adds roughly $5 to $11 a month. Some systems also charge for equipment or setup.

faq.q: Does fall detection always work?
faq.a: No. No device catches every fall. Studies cited by NCOA put average accuracy at roughly 80% to 93%. Always press the button yourself if you can, and test the device regularly.

faq.q: Does Medicare pay for a medical alert system?
faq.a: Original Medicare does not. Some Medicare Advantage plans offer partial help, some state Medicaid waiver programs cover them, and veterans may be able to get help through the VA. Ask your plan, your Area Agency on Aging, or the VA.

faq.q: What is a stove shutoff device?
faq.a: It is a device that turns off the stove or cuts its power if it has been left on too long or no one is in the kitchen. It can help when memory problems make it easy to forget a pot. Cooking is the leading cause of home fires.

faq.q: Are smart home cameras a privacy risk?

body_md:
Technology cannot replace a safe home or a caring person. But the right tools can help an older adult call for help, see who is at the door, and avoid common accidents. This guide covers the main types of tools, what they cost, and the privacy questions to ask. We do not recommend brands.

## Why it matters

In AARP's 2024 survey, **64%** of adults 50 and older said they expect to need a medical alert system, and **44%** said they need smart security features [1]. CDC also suggests older adults consider a device that lets them call for help after a fall, and keep a phone where they could reach it from the floor [2].

The reason is simple. A fall is much more dangerous when no one knows it happened.

## Medical alert systems

### What they are

A **medical alert system**, also called a **personal emergency response system (PERS)**, lets you call for help by pressing a button. You usually wear the button as a pendant, wristband or watch.

### Main types

- **In-home systems.** A base unit connects to a phone line or cell network. The button works inside the home and sometimes the yard.
- **Mobile systems.** A small device with a cell connection and GPS. It works away from home, too.
- **Smartwatch-style systems.** A watch that can call for help and may track activity.
- **Monitored vs. unmonitored.** Monitored systems connect you to a call center 24/7. Unmonitored ones call family or 911 directly. Monitored systems cost more but someone always answers.

### Typical costs

A 2025 review by the National Council on Aging (NCOA) found [3]:

- **Monthly fees** from about **$19.95 to $159.95**, not counting fall detection.
- **Fall detection** usually adds about **$5 to $11 a month**. Some plans include it.
- **Upfront equipment costs** range from none to a few hundred dollars, depending on the device.

Ask about activation fees, equipment fees, cancellation fees, and whether the price goes up after a trial period.

### Fall detection: helpful, not perfect

Some devices sense a hard fall and call for help on their own. That can help if a person is knocked out or too hurt to press a button.

But **no fall detector is 100% accurate** [3]. Research cited by NCOA puts average accuracy at about **80% to 93%** [3]. Devices can also send false alarms, for example if dropped [3].

So: **press the button yourself** whenever you can, and **test the device** on a regular schedule [3].

### Tips for choosing

- **Will it actually be worn?** The best device is the one worn in the shower and at night. A slippery tub and a dark trip to the bathroom are classic fall risks [2].
- **Is it waterproof?**
- **How long does the battery last,** and how will you know when it is low?
- **Does it work where the person goes?** Home only, or out and about?
- **Can you test it** without paying extra?
- **Is there a long contract?**

### Who pays?

- **Original Medicare does not cover** medical alert systems [4].
- **Some Medicare Advantage plans** offer partial coverage [4].
- **Medicaid** may cover them through home and community-based services (HCBS) waiver programs in some states [4].
- **Veterans** may be able to get a discounted or free system through the VA [4].

Ask your Area Agency on Aging about local programs.

### Watch out for "free" medical alert offers

Be careful with calls promising a "free" system. The FTC and Florida's attorney general sued a company that made **at least a billion robocalls** telling people a medical alert device had been paid for and was "free." People later found they owed monthly fees and faced penalties for canceling [5]. Hang up on robocalls. Buy only after you have read the contract.

## Smart home tools

### Smart and motion-sensor lighting

**What it does:** Lights that turn on when you walk in, on a schedule, or by voice.

**Why it helps:** Dark stairs and a dark path to the bathroom at night are common fall risks. CDC advises night-lights and lighting you can turn on without walking in the dark [2].

**Typical cost:** Plug-in motion night-lights and smart bulbs are usually low cost. Hard-wired motion switches may need an electrician.

### Voice assistants and smart speakers

**What they do:** Turn lights on and off, set reminders, make calls, and play music by voice.

**Why they help:** Useful for people with limited hand use or vision. Some can call a family member by voice. Do not rely on one as your only way to get help, since many cannot call 911 directly.

### Video doorbells

**What they do:** Let you see and talk to whoever is at the door from a phone or screen, without opening it.

**Why they help:** They make it easier to turn away door-to-door salespeople and scam artists. Family members can also see who is visiting, with permission. See our guide to [home repair scams](/guides/home-repair-scams-seniors).

**Typical cost:** A one-time device cost, plus an optional monthly fee to save video.

### Stove shutoff and kitchen safety devices

**What they do:** Turn off the stove, or cut its power, if it has been on too long or no one is moving in the kitchen.

**Why they help:** **Cooking is the leading cause of home fires and home fire injuries** [6]. **Unattended equipment** is the top factor in kitchen fires that spread beyond the pan [6]. Adults 65 and older were **2.5 times** as likely to die in a home fire as the overall population in 2020 [7]. A shutoff device can help when memory problems make it easy to forget a pot.

**Typical cost:** Varies. Some plug in; others need an electrician, especially for electric ranges. Gas stoves need special models.

A simple timer is the low-cost first step [7].

### Smart smoke and carbon monoxide alarms

**What they do:** Send an alert to your phone, or a family member's, when the alarm sounds.

**Why they help:** Family can know about a problem even when they are far away. For people who cannot hear a regular alarm, there are alarms with **bed shakers or strobe lights** [7].

### Water leak and temperature sensors

**What they do:** Alert you to leaks, freezing pipes or a home that is too hot or cold.

**Why they help:** They catch problems before they turn into slippery floors, mold or dangerous heat.

### Activity and check-in sensors

**What they do:** Motion or door sensors learn a person's normal routine and alert family if something seems off, such as no movement in the kitchen by mid-morning.

**Why they help:** They offer peace of mind without cameras. They are not emergency devices.

### Medication reminders and dispensers

**What they do:** Beep, light up or unlock the right pills at the right time, and can alert family if a dose is missed.

**Why they help:** Missed or doubled doses can cause dizziness and falls.

## Privacy and security

Any device that connects to the internet can be a privacy risk. Follow these steps:

1. **Talk first, and get consent.** The older adult should agree to every device, especially cameras and sensors. Being watched without consent can damage trust.
2. **Keep cameras out of private spaces** like bedrooms and bathrooms. Use motion or door sensors there if needed.
3. **Use long, unique passwords** for every account, and store them in a password manager [8].
4. **Turn on two-step login (multifactor authentication)** whenever it is offered [8].
5. **Turn on automatic updates** so devices get security fixes [8].
6. **Watch for phishing.** Don't click links in surprise texts or emails about your device or account [8].
7. **Read what data is collected** and who it is shared with. Pick settings that share the least.
8. **Decide who gets alerts.** Only people the older adult trusts.

## Where to start

1. **Begin with low-cost basics:** night-lights, a phone within reach of the floor, and working smoke alarms [2][7].
2. **Add a medical alert system** if the person lives alone, has fallen, or has health conditions that raise fall risk.
3. **Add smart tools one at a time,** and make sure the person is comfortable using each one.
4. **Check for help paying** through Medicaid waivers, Medicare Advantage, the VA or your state assistive technology program. Call the Eldercare Locator at 1-800-677-1116.
